extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, public administrators, civics students, and interested members of the public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for organizing, running, and evaluating public consultations (public comment, town halls, deliberative assemblies, surveys, participatory budgeting). Covers methods, sampling/representativeness, procedural rules, and common criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of public consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation's main goals are to improve public involvement and influence, as well as the transparency and efficiency of government projects, laws, or regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consultation to increase democratic legitimacy, let citizens learn about policy issues, surface preferences and trade-offs, and improve policy by integrating public input into decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification / publicising the consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation usually involves notification (to publicize the matter to be consulted on).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, timely notices through multiple channels (newspaper, web, mail to known interested parties) including a notice of completion for drafts; ensure stakeholders and the general public are informed of opportunities to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation as two-way information exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation is a two-way flow of information and opinion exchange between authorities and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design processes that allow officials to both provide information and meaningfully receive, consider, and respond to public input rather than only transmitting information one-way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation / stakeholder involvement in drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation involves stakeholders in the drafting of policy or legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, involve affected stakeholders directly in drafting stages (e.g., workshops, advisory groups) to increase buy-in and the relevance of changes; be transparent about how participation influences outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of background information and opportunity for deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: All consultation methods involve the provision of background information on the issue, and the opportunity for deliberation on the regulation, law or plan under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide balanced briefing materials and opportunities (face-to-face or structured online) for participants to discuss pros/cons, ask questions of experts, and reflect before submitting views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling is required to generalize to the population
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only through representative samples that one can use the findings of a public consultation to characterize the distribution of views in the general population including the identification of majority views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the objective is to measure public opinion or identify majority views, use representative sampling methods rather than relying on self-selected participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to achieve representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: To achieve a representative sample the ideal method is a purely random selection of the population, but reasonably representative samples can still be achieved by opt-in samples by stratifying the sample in advance and weighting it afterwards according to key demographic variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer random selection/sortition. If using opt-in panels, plan stratification, weighting, and ensure sampling frames lack obvious biases; document methodology and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment period procedures and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: A public comment period is established and comments which are received by the cutoff date become part of the official public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear start/end dates, make it explicit that comments become part of the record, provide easily accessible submission channels, and maintain searchable archives/portals for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirements to respond or incorporate comments
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, there is a statutory mandate that those comments be replied to or incorporated in some fashion into the Final document in advance of the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where law requires, provide formal responses showing how input was considered and whether/how it was incorporated; document reasons for accepting or rejecting suggestions to enhance accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and low barrier participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Email, surveys, and social media offer relatively accessible forms of consultation, lowering the barriers of time and travel required to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer multiple accessible participation channels (online, mail, in-person, telephone), consider language and disability access, and provide clear instructions to maximize genuine participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of illegitimate feedback (automation / AI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2023 report cautions that AI-generated text (such as from bots on social media) may result in illegitimate feedback in addition to legitimate testimony and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement safeguards against automated or coordinated inauthentic submissions (captcha, identity verification where appropriate, automated detection for bot-like content) and document how such inputs are handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between open public meetings and selected hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Common instances of public meetings include town halls open to all, while public hearings are not open to all and participants are selected by the governing body due to their expertise or representation of stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the meeting format intentionally: use open town halls for broad input, and targeted hearings for expert/stakeholder testimony; explain selection criteria for invited participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative assemblies / mini-public design features
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberative assemblies are usually representative samples (mini-publics), often achieved by sortition; they are briefed by experts, have discussions, and vote on some type of final recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When convening mini-publics, use rigorous recruitment (random stratified selection), balanced briefing materials, independent facilitation, and clear processes for deliberation and producing recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public consultation surveys as self-contained deliberative tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation surveys are surveys where the entirety of the deliberative process takes place within the survey: respondents are provided relevant briefing materials, and arguments for and against various proposals and then provide their final recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design survey instruments with balanced briefings, clear questions about trade-offs, and sufficiently large representative samples; document materials and the way recommendations are elicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative opinion polling methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberative opinion polling combines surveys of a representative sample with face-to-face deliberation: the sample is surveyed in advance, briefed, engages in deliberation with expert presentations, and then is re-surveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre/post measurement to capture how informed deliberation affects opinions; include neutral expert presentations and structured small-group discussion to avoid domination by particular voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participatory budgeting as a decision-making process
rubrics_metrics.description: Participatory budgeting involves a sample of ordinary people, sometimes representative, making decisions about their government's budget through a process of democratic deliberation and decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify scale, scope, and rules (who decides, what budget items are eligible), ensure representativeness where required, and specify whether processes are legally mandated or NGO-led; document how recommendations translate into budgetary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency via comment portals and ability to review others' submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A government portal may allow review of comments and opportunity for making comment and can be searched by keyword; comments received become part of the official record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide searchable public access to submissions where privacy permits, and consider whether participants can view others' comments before submitting (this can affect deliberation dynamics and should be disclosed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common criticisms: unrepresentativeness and domination by particular demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous studies have shown that public consultation meetings tend to be unrepresentative of the general population, with meetings dominated by older, wealthier, whiter residents and homeowners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess participant demographics, mitigate bias through outreach or representative methods, report participant composition, and be cautious about generalizing from self-selected meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: consultations can delay or hinder projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation is also controversial for its role in hindering and delaying development and infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance inclusive consultation with clear timelines and procedures to avoid undue delay; set expectations about how input will affect scheduling and project decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of manipulation / biased question design by authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultations can be manipulated to push the government's ideology or agenda with suggestive questions (example: national questionnaires using leading language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral, balanced question wording; disclose question design and testing; guard against framing that steers respondents toward a predetermined answer; provide avenues for independent scrutiny.
